title: Ubiquitous topological materials protected by hidden partial symmetries
authors: Lumen Eek, Xuelong Chen, Malte Röntgen, Wenlong Gao, Cristiane Morais Smith
abstract: Symmetries play a crucial role in protecting the topological phases of insulators, ensuring the robustness of their surface states against perturbations. Traditionally, these symmetries have to be obeyed by the system as a whole, which is a rather strong constraint. In this work, we demonstrate that topological effects can also be realized through a substantially weaker form of symmetry that we coin \emph{partial latent symmetries}. For these, invariance is required only at certain energy scales of an effective Hamiltonian, rather than for the object as a whole. Applying this idea, we construct weak-symmetry versions of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes models. These weak-symmetry models behave in many aspects just like their conventional brethren---in particular, they host robust edge states---, though the corresponding topological invariants are only \emph{approximately} quantized. We conclude this work by experimentally realizing Hermitian and non-Hermitian versions of such approximate topological insulators and probe their edge states. Overall, given the ubiquity of symmetry in all areas of physics and engineering, we foresee our work to serve as a cornerstone for exploring how conventional, strong symmetry requirements can be replaced by weak-symmetry ones.
summary: This paper introduces the concept of 'partial latent symmetries,' allowing topological protection to be guaranteed by symmetry only at specific energy scales rather than globally. The authors demonstrate this concept using modified SSH and BBH models, showing that these weak symmetries can stabilize robust edge and corner states, which are experimentally verified in non-Hermitian circuits.
main_problem: The work addresses the limitation of traditional topological protection, which requires strong, global symmetries, by proposing a weaker concept: partial latent symmetries.
main_result: Topological effects, such as robust edge and corner states, can be realized using partial latent symmetries, leading to topological invariants that are only approximately quantized.
method: The authors construct weak-symmetry versions of known models (like SSH and BBH) and analyze their properties using concepts like the Inverse Scattering Relation (ISR) and by testing robustness against disorder.
model_or_system: The study applies to lattice models, including the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) and Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes (BBH) models, extended to Hermitian and non-Hermitian variants. These are realized both computationally (tight-binding Hamiltonians) and experimentally using electric circuits.
key_observables: Edge states, corner-localized states, Zak phase (quantization), topological invariants (approximately quantized), and impedance spectra resonance.
important_parameters: Energy scales ($E$) at which symmetry is required, disorder strength ($D$), and hopping/potential parameters ($t, v, \Delta$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that partial latent symmetries can stabilize topological features, even if the corresponding invariants are only approximately quantized. The ISR requires pruning stub sites for well-defined calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the progression from conventional to partial latent symmetries (Fig. 1), compare edge states in symmetric vs. partial latent cases (Fig. 2), show 2D realizations and corner modes (Fig. 3), and finally demonstrate the robustness of these states against disorder (Figs. S12, S13).
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the concept of partial latent symmetry, applies it to 1D models (SSH), extends it to 2D models (BBH), and culminates in experimental realizations using non-Hermitian circuits to test robustness against disorder.
why_interesting: This work provides a generalized framework for topological physics, suggesting that physical systems can exhibit topological protection under much weaker symmetry constraints than previously assumed, which is highly relevant for designing novel quantum materials and circuits.
